# Sample Mean and SD ## Sample Proportion Review ::: {#exm-sample-prop1} A researcher randomly surveys 200 college students and finds that 64 of them own a car. Which of the following statements is correct? (a) The sample proportion $\hat{p} = 0.32$. (b) The population proportion is $p = 0.32$. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer (a) is correct since we have taken a sample. ::: ::: {#exm-sample-prop2} Suppose 40% of all adults in a large city use public transit at least once a week. You take a random sample of 150 adults and let $\hat{p}$ be the proportion in the sample who use public transit weekly. Which correctly describes the distribution of $\hat{p}$? (a) Approximately Normal, mean $= 0.40$, standard deviation $= 0.04$ (b) Approximately Normal, mean $= 0.40$, standard deviation $= 0.0016$ (c) Approximately Normal, mean $= 0.40$, standard deviation $= 0.24$ ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Answer (a) is correct. The standard deviation of the distribution is given by the formula, $$\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.4(0.6)}{150}} = 0.04.$$ ::: ::: {#exm-sample-prop3} At a researcher's university, 20% of all students are first-generation college students. The researcher takes a random sample of 400 students is selected, and $\hat{p}$ is the proportion of first-generation students in the sample. What is the probability that the sample proportion is less than 0.17? ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer We can assume $\hat{p}$ is distributed normally since $np \geq 10$ and $n(1-p) \geq 10$. The mean is $0.2$ and the standard deviation is $$\sqrt{\frac{0.2(0.8)}{400}} = 0.02.$$ Now we can use the normal calculator to compute $P(\hat{p} < 0.17) = 0.0668$. ::: ## Sample Mean Now we will focus on questions with *quantitative data*. In these instances, we want to compare the **sample mean** with the **population mean**. ::: {#exm-sample-mean} A deli wants to know how long customers typically wait in line for their order. To measure this, the deli randomly samples 50 customers throughout the week. They find that the average wait time of these 50 customers was 7.25 minutes. This is the **sample mean**, e.g. $\bar{x} = 7.5$ minutes. ::: Like the sample proportion, the sample mean is a random variable. If I choose a different sample of customers in the example above, I should not expect the sample mean to be the same. Under the *right conditions*. We should expect the sample mean to be approximately normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, where $\sigma$ is the population standard deviation and $n$ is the sample size.

What do we mean by *right conditions*?

If our random sample size is large enough, then we can assume the distribution of sample means is approximately normal. The general rule of thumb is if $n \geq 30$ we can assume the distribution is normal. ::: {#exm-sample-mean2} In a certain state, the average teacher salary is $54,000 with a standard deviation of $5,000. If I sample 50 teachers randomly, what is the probability that my sample mean is greater than $56,000? Before we compute the answer, we should recognize that $\mu = 54,000$ and $\sigma = 5,000$ are the population mean and standard deviation, respectively. Additionally, the sample size $n = 50$. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer Since my sample size is 50, this is large enough to assume the sample mean is distributed normally. The standard deviation is then: $$ \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{5000}{\sqrt{50}} = 707.107$$ Now we can use the normal calculator to compute $P(\bar{x} > 56,000) = 0.0023$. ::: ::: {#exm-sample-mean3} The average time for pizza delivery at a pizzeria is 36 minutes with a standard deviation of 8 minutes. If 30 customers are sampled, what is the probability that the average wait time of those customers will be between 34 and 38 minutes? ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer Since my sample size is 30, this is large enough to assume the sample mean is distributed normally. The standard deviation is then: $$ \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{30}} = 1.26$$ Now we can use the normal calculator to compute $P(34 <\bar{x} < 38) = 0.8876$. ::: If our sample size is *not* at least 30, then we can use the normal approximation only if our *population* is distributed normally. We should not assume that our *population* distribution is normal unless we are told it is. Note that this reveals an important and some times confusing fact: the population may have any distribution, but as long as our sample size is large enough the sample mean is **always** normal. This is again thanks to the **Central Limit Theorem**! [We can explore the central limit theorem here.](https://central-limit-visualizer.replit.app/){target="blank"} ::: {#exm-sample-mean3} The average number of pets in a household is 1.4. If I randomly sample 8 households, what is the probability that the sample mean is less than 1? ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer **We do not have enough information to answer this!** We should not assume the number of pets in a household is normally distributed. In fact, we would expect it to be a skewed distribution. ::: ::: {#exm-sample-mean4} The weight of a newborn baby is approximately normally distributed with a mean of 3.4 kg and a standard deviation of 0.5 kg. If I sample 4 newborn babies, what is the probability their average weight is between 3.3 and 3.5 kg? ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer While our sample size is small, since the weight of newborns is approximately normal we are okay to use a normal approximation for the sample mean. First we compute the standard deviation: $$ \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.5}{\sqrt{4}} = 0.25$$ Now use the normal calculator to compute, $P(3.3 < \bar{x} < 3.5) = 0.3108$. ::: ## Mixed Practice ### Problem 1 For each scenario, state whether the statistic of interest is a sample mean ($\bar{x}$) or a sample proportion ($\hat{p}$). a. A city planner records the commute time (in minutes) of 50 randomly selected workers. b. A pollster asks 800 randomly selected voters whether they support a ballot measure. c. A quality inspector tests 200 light bulbs and counts how many are defective. d. An advisor records the GPA of 40 randomly selected seniors. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer a. Sample mean. b. Sample proportion. c. Sample proportion. d. Sample mean. **Guide:** If you measure a number for each individual, use $\bar{x}$. If you classify each individual into a category, use $\hat{p}$. ::: ### Problem 2 For each situation, decide whether the sampling distribution of the statistic is approximately Normal. Justify your answer. a. 4% of products from a factory are defective. A random sample of 150 products is selected, and $\hat{p}$ is the proportion defective. b. Household incomes in a city are strongly skewed right. A random sample of 12 households is selected, and $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean income. c. Adult female heights are normally distributed. A random sample of 8 women is selected, and $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean height. d. The time customers spend in a store is skewed right. A random sample of 50 customers is selected, and $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean time. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Answer a. Not appropriate, $np = 150(0.04) = 6 < 10$, so the large counts condition fails. b. Not appropriate, the population is strongly skewed and $n = 12 < 30$, so the Central Limit Theorem does not apply. c. Appropriate, the population is Normal, so $\bar{x}$ is Normal for *any* sample size. d. Appropriate, although the population is skewed, $n = 50 \geq 30$, so the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately Normal. ::: ### Problem 3 A coffee machine fills cups with an amount of coffee that is Normally distributed with mean $\mu = 12$ ounces and standard deviation $\sigma = 0.4$ ounces. A random sample of 16 cups is selected. What is the probability that the sample mean amount of coffee is less than 11.8 ounces? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution Despite the fact that the sample size is only 16, since the population distribution is normal, we can assume the distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal. The mean of $\bar{x}$ is the population mean, which is 12. The standard deviation of $\bar{x}$ is $$ \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.4}{\sqrt{16}} = 0.1. $$ Now we can compute the probability, $$ P(\bar{x} < 11.8) \approx 0.0228 $$ ::: ### Problem 4: Probability for $\bar{x}$ (Central Limit Theorem) The number of hours students at a large high school spend on homework per night is skewed right, with mean $\mu = 3.2$ hours and standard deviation $\sigma = 1.8$ hours. A random sample of 36 students is selected. What is the probability that the sample mean is between 2.9 and 3.5 hours? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution **Conditions:** - *Random:* The sample is random. - *10% condition:* 36 is less than 10% of all students at a large high school. - *Shape:* The population is skewed, but $n = 36 \geq 30$, so by the Central Limit Theorem the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately Normal. **Center and spread:** $$ \mu_{\bar{x}} = 3.2 \qquad \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{1.8}{\sqrt{36}} = 0.3 $$ **Standardize:** $$ z_1 = \frac{2.9 - 3.2}{0.3} = -1 \qquad z_2 = \frac{3.5 - 3.2}{0.3} = 1 $$ **Probability:** $$ P(2.9 < \bar{x} < 3.5) = P(-1 < Z < 1) \approx 0.6827 $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} se <- 1.8 / sqrt(36) pnorm(3.5, mean = 3.2, sd = se) - pnorm(2.9, mean = 3.2, sd = se) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6826895 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Problem 5: Probability for $\hat{p}$ A grocery chain reports that 36% of its customers use its loyalty app. A random sample of 225 customers is selected. What is the probability that more than 40% of the sampled customers use the loyalty app? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution **Conditions:** - *Random:* The sample is random. - *10% condition:* 225 is less than 10% of all the chain's customers. - *Large counts:* $$ np = 225(0.36) = 81 \geq 10 \qquad n(1-p) = 225(0.64) = 144 \geq 10 $$ So the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is approximately Normal. **Center and spread:** $$ \mu_{\hat{p}} = 0.36 \qquad \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.36(0.64)}{225}} = \sqrt{0.001024} = 0.032 $$ **Standardize:** $$ z = \frac{0.40 - 0.36}{0.032} = 1.25 $$ **Probability:** $$ P(\hat{p} > 0.40) = P(Z > 1.25) \approx 0.1056 $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pnorm(0.40, mean = 0.36, sd = sqrt(0.36 * 0.64 / 225), lower.tail = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1056498 ``` ::: ::: :::
